title: Code Tour — how a repository becomes a tour, and how the tour stays true
audience: engineer picking up maintenance of this skill
orientation: Three scripts run in pipeline order: propose candidate stops, render and audit the notes, then validate the anchors against the tree. Read them in that order — each one assumes the output of the last. Nothing here touches a network or a database, so you can run every stop locally as you read it.
prerequisites: Run scripts/tour_propose.py --repo scripts --max-stops 3 first, so you have seen the output the rest of the pipeline consumes

stops.title: Why role classification reads path components, not the path string
stops.read_first: The TEST_DIRS set and TEST_FILE_RE pattern above the function.
stops.note: An earlier version substring-matched hints against the whole relative path, which meant any repository with 'spec' or 'test' in a directory name had its entire source tree classified as tests and excluded from the tour. Matching against path components and a filename regex instead keeps the signal while removing the false positives, at the cost of missing unconventional test layouts — a trade worth taking, because a tour missing a stop is recoverable and a tour proposing nothing is not.
stops.question: What happens to a file at src/api/testing_utils.py? Trace both the TEST_DIRS and TEST_FILE_RE branches.
stops.gotcha: Boundary hints match on tokens split from the stem, so payment_handler.py is a boundary but paymenthandler.py is not.

stops.title: Two fan-in strategies, and why the weaker one still ships
stops.note: Python fan-in is computed from the real AST import graph and is trustworthy. Everything else falls back to counting filename references in quotes, which over-counts common stems like index or utils. Shipping the weak heuristic rather than refusing to rank non-Python repositories is deliberate: the output is a shortlist a human curates, not a verdict, so a noisy ranking still beats alphabetical order.
stops.question: Why does the AST walk collect alias names from ImportFrom as well as the module name?

stops.title: How the renderer detects a note that explains nothing
stops.read_first: WHAT_ONLY_RE and WHY_MARKERS above the function.
stops.note: The audit is three cheap heuristics rather than anything semantic, because the failure it catches is blunt: notes that open by restating what the code does, notes too short to carry reasoning, and notes with no causal language at all. It will pass a well-phrased note that says nothing, and that is accepted — the goal is to catch the author who described behaviour on autopilot, not to grade prose.
stops.question: Which of the three checks would fire on the note you are reading right now?
stops.gotcha: A note can pass the audit and still be wrong. The audit checks shape, never truth.

stops.title: The whole thesis: anchors resolve by symbol, not by line
stops.note: Tours here survive refactoring because of this resolution step. Python anchors resolve through the AST, so a stop keeps working after the file is reformatted, grows by 200 lines, or has the function moved within it — none of which a line number survives. Non-Python falls back to first-line text search, which is weaker but still immune to edits above the anchor. The recorded line is output, never identity.
stops.question: Why does the fallback branch return a 20-line window rather than a single line?

stops.title: A stop that has since moved
stops.note: Included deliberately so the validator has a deleted anchor to report against this very package. Real tours accumulate these within weeks, because the code moves and the tour does not follow it unless something forces the issue — which is the entire reason validation runs in CI rather than on request.

after: Run the three scripts in pipeline order against this skill's own directory: propose stops from scripts/, render this tour with --audit-only, then validate it. Stop 5 fails the note audit and stop 6 fails validation, both on purpose — every finding path is exercised by the sample.
